It's the best choice for them not to play. Back when GamerGate was in full swing, feminists and the like were initiating damage control left and right. Considering that a large portion of them run inflated blogs, this means that anyone who outright doesn't support them but comments them has to deal with mah soggy knees. Not every publisher is Rockstar, and dealing with the image of being on-the-edge counterculture topics in their games, so the marketing and public relations departments, not wanting their general-audience kid friendly action game, don't want to be associated with women bashing.

On the other hand, coming out against GamerGate wouldn't have really done much good for them because the people who would view that as favorable outcome are completely marginal to the amount of people who that would offset. If you think I just contradicted myself to the previous point, consider that "Ubisoft, developer of the upcoming Rayman Legends 2, sides with bigoted terrorist group" gets more clicks than "Ubisoft, developer of the upcoming Rayman Legends 2, sides with equality." Siding with equality and human rights isn't anything worth garnering attention, so the attempt to equate anti-Gamer ideology with pro-equaltiy falls, as the brief explanation of what GamerGate is causes no favor to the hypothetical Ubisoft because the implications become then that the publisher is allied with the author of the article, which does jack-all for the hypoethical Ubisoft.

(The exception to this are indie games that are so piss poor that no significant amount of people would buy them, so they shoehorn in some SJW bullshit to capture that dogmatic, albeit minute, audience).

Finally, there's the relationship between the publisher and journalist that takes a toll from this decision if made positive - most mainstream games by some major publishers are either going to be extraordinarily praised beyond what they deserve because hype (Fallout 4, Mass Effect...) or bashed (Sonic), so having for example a hypothetical Ubisoft side with GamerGate means that all of that free, easy, and unfair hype is lost. The counterpoint to this is that the effects of online bloggers (it pained me to call them "journalists") are diminishing on the general audience, but the likes of Metacritic and GameInformer (which is heavily advertised by one of the largest game retailers today) are so ingrained into the mainstream that we still have some time before the transition with the mainstream audience from printed to video content is complete. Although some of the major reviewers are starting to notice this and offer video content, we still have some time before that transition is complete. I'd wager at least one holiday season, which means the short term risk isn't as profitable to them.

Large companies try and avoid controversy.

They don't always succeed (Konami basically self destructed last year, and Nintendo has gone through hell due to a ton of bad decisions on the PR/marketing front), but GamerGate is hugely controversial. And if there's one thing a company fears, it's being in the middle of a media shitstorm because they said something that could be seen as 'edgy' or 'wrong'. They know that if they take sides here, they will get it in the neck for months. If they come out for it, the SJWs will basically tear them to pieces for the next year and a half or so, and cause a ton of bad publicity. If they come out against it, then a large percentage of non SJWs will tear them to pieces for the next year and a half or so, and they'll get struck with boycotts and stuff.

Better for their reputation and sales to keep quiet and hope that they don't get asked to make a statement about it.
